transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello. Thank you for fitting me in. It's, um, it's a bit of a long story, but I guess the main reason I'm here is... well, it has to do with the local historical society. I've been involved with them for a little while, just to keep busy since I haven't been working, you know? We try to do these little community events. But recently we had this big fundraiser coming up, and I just—I completely took over the whole project. 

I mean, I was acting like I could run the entire fundraiser all by myself. I just dove right in. I started sketching out all these incredibly complex quilt designs for the auction, just drawing up pattern after pattern, thinking I could sew them all myself. And while I was doing that, I was on the phone constantly, calling every single volunteer on our roster. I had my big notebook out, making these massive, detailed schedules for everyone, assigning shifts and tasks. I was going to meetings and promising the board all these deadlines that... well, looking back, I couldn't possibly meet. I told them I'd have everything organized, the quilts finished, the venue sorted out in just a matter of days. And you have to understand, quilting takes a tremendous amount of time, it's not something you just whip up in an afternoon, but I was just so absolutely sure I could do it all. I was just so focused on getting it all done, and I guess my family thought my behavior was getting to be a bit too much, which is why they pushed me to come see you today.
Did you feel unusually happy or excited during the time you were working on the fundraiser?

Well, yes and no. It’s funny you ask it like that, because at first... oh, at first it was just this incredible feeling. I felt almost glowing, honestly. It was like every single idea that popped into my head was just absolutely wonderful, brilliant even. I’d be sitting there with my sketchpad, and the colors and patterns for the quilts would just flow out of me, and I felt so light and energized and just... happy. More than happy, really. I felt like I was doing exactly what I was meant to be doing, and it was all going to be perfect. 

But then... well, the problem was other people. You see, when you have that much clarity and you know exactly how something should be done, it’s very frustrating when people don't see the vision. If anyone on the committee questioned me—like, if Mary asked if maybe we needed more time to source the fabric, or if Susan suggested we scale back the number of auction items—I just... I got so snappish. I really did. I would just snap right back at them because, in my mind, they were just standing in the way of progress. I felt like I was driving this train at top speed, and they were all just throwing rocks on the tracks. So, I was very excited, yes, but I also had absolutely zero patience for anyone who wasn't moving as fast as I was.
Did you ever feel unhappy or sad during this highly energetic and productive period?

No, no, I wouldn't say I felt sad. Not at all. It's funny, because usually when I'm, you know, not feeling quite right, sadness is a big part of it, but during this whole fundraiser situation, sadness was the furthest thing from my mind. I mean, I was just so propelled forward, if that makes sense. Like I said, I was either feeling absolutely fantastic, just on top of the world with all these brilliant ideas for the quilts and the auction, or I was just incredibly irritated that nobody else could keep up with me. 

There was no room for sadness. I didn't have time to be sad! I was too busy coordinating everything, making those schedules, calling people. I remember one afternoon, I was sitting at my kitchen table—which was completely covered in fabric swatches and lists, by the way, just a total mess, but an organized mess in my head—and my daughter came over and she looked so concerned. She asked if I was feeling okay, and I just laughed. I told her I had never felt better, never been more productive. Why would I be sad when I was accomplishing so much? It was only when people like Mary or Susan started dragging their feet that I felt anything negative, and that was just pure frustration, not unhappiness. So, no, sadness wasn't part of it during that specific time. Just that high energy and then the irritation when things didn't go exactly as I planned.
How long did this feeling of being 'on top of the world' with all these brilliant ideas last?

Well, let me think about that, because time gets so funny when you're moving that fast, doesn't it? It feels like it was just a whirlwind, but when I actually sit down and look at the calendar and trace it back to when I first started sketching out those initial quilt designs—which, by the way, were based on some 19th-century patterns I found in the society's archives, just beautiful intricate geometric shapes that I thought would look absolutely stunning in modern fabrics—anyway, from that first spark of an idea all the way through to when I just couldn't keep it up anymore, it was quite a long stretch. 

I'd say that whole overdriven period, where I was just buzzing with ideas and trying to run the entire historical society project single-handedly, that went on for about five months. Yes, five whole months of just constant motion, constant planning, waking up at three in the morning because I had a sudden revelation about the seating chart for the fundraiser or a new color scheme for the silent auction items. I mean, five months is a long time to sustain that kind of energy, and honestly, looking back, I don't know how my body handled it. I was barely stopping to eat a proper meal, just grabbing a piece of toast while I was on the phone with the caterers or the venue managers. And of course, that's when the friction with the other committee members really started to build up, because they were moving at a normal, five-month pace, and I was trying to cram five months of work into every single week. So, yes, it was about a five-month stretch before everything finally just... fell apart.
Was there ever a time during those five months when you didn't feel 'on top of the world' or extremely energetic?

Well, it’s hard to say exactly, because when you’re in the middle of something like that, you don't really take inventory of every single day, you know? It’s not like I kept a diary saying, "Today I feel 100% energetic, today I only feel 90%." But if I really try to pull it apart and look at those five months... I mean, I guess there must have been moments where I wasn't completely flying high, but honestly, I don't remember them. 

The whole period just blurs together into this one long, continuous surge of electricity. Even when I was physically exhausted—like, I remember one time my hands were actually cramping from cutting so much fabric, and my eyes were burning from staring at the computer screen trying to format the auction catalog—even then, my brain was still just racing. I didn't feel tired in my head, if that makes sense. I didn't have any days where I woke up and thought, "Oh, I just can't do this today." Never. Not once. Every morning, or middle of the night, really, I was just ready to go, go, go. 

So, no, I can't recall a single day or even an afternoon where that intense energy dropped off. It was just a constant, driving force until the very end when the crash finally happened. But during those five months? No, it was all just high gear, all the time.
You mentioned the crash finally happened at the end, can you describe what you mean by 'the crash'?

Oh, the crash. Well, it was just... it was awful. It was like hitting a brick wall at a hundred miles an hour. You see, because I had pushed everyone so hard, and I had taken on so much myself, things eventually just started slipping through the cracks. The fabric orders for the quilts got hopelessly behind schedule because I had miscalculated the yardage—which I never do, I'm usually so meticulous with my measurements—but I had ordered the wrong backing material for three of the largest pieces. And then the conflicts with the other volunteers just blew up entirely. Mary actually quit the committee, and Susan sent this scathing email to the historical society board about my "dictatorial" management style. 

When all of that happened, when the reality of the mess I'd made finally caught up with me... the energy just vanished. Poof. Gone. And since then, since all those orders fell behind and the volunteer situation just completely blew up in my face, I’ve just been stuck. I’ve been stuck in this incredibly low, heavy, guilty place. It’s like I can’t forgive myself for ruining the project and alienating my friends. And this feeling, this awful, paralyzing sadness and guilt... it’s been dragging on for about nine months now. Nine months of just feeling like I'm moving through molasses, barely able to look at my sewing machine without wanting to cry. It's just been nine months of this total, crushing low.
Did the feeling of being stuck in a low, heavy, guilty place start immediately after the crash or was there a delay?

Well, it was pretty much immediate, really. I mean, the minute I read that email from Susan—the one she copied the entire board on, if you can believe it—it was like a switch flipped. The energy didn't just fade away, it was just instantly replaced by this... this crushing weight. 

And ever since that exact moment, I just... I can't stop thinking about it. I keep going over every single late fabric order, every wrong measurement, every sharp, impatient thing I said to Mary and Susan and the other volunteers. I mean, I replay those conversations in my head constantly, analyzing my tone of voice and how I must have sounded so arrogant and dismissive when they were just trying to help. It’s like a broken record in my mind. I just sit there in my sewing room—well, I don't sew anymore, I just sit in the chair—and I tell myself over and over how I completely ruined everything. I let the church down, because they were counting on those quilts for the charity raffle, and I let the historical society down after they trusted me with their archives, and honestly, I feel like I've let this whole town down. It’s a small community, you know? Everyone knows everyone, and everyone knows what a spectacular mess I made of the bicentennial project. So, yes, the guilt and that heavy feeling started right then and there, the second the whole thing collapsed, and it just hasn't let up for a single day since.
Did you expect to feel as low and guilty as you do now after the project fell apart, or did the intensity of these feelings surprise you?

Well, I suppose... I mean, I knew I would feel bad, of course. Anyone would feel bad when a project they were leading falls apart. But the sheer intensity of it? No, I never saw this coming. It’s not just feeling disappointed or embarrassed, it’s this absolute, all-consuming conviction that I am just a terrible, incompetent person. 

I really didn't expect it to take over my brain the way it has. Like I was saying, I just keep going over every single late order, every yard of fabric I messed up, and every sharp, awful thing I said to the volunteers. It’s like my brain won't let me rest. I sit there and I tell myself, over and over, how I let the church down, how I let the historical society down, and honestly, how I let this entire town down. Because everybody knows. In a town this size, everybody knows exactly what happened with the bicentennial auction. 

And it’s the guilt that really surprises me—the depth of it. It’s not just "Oh, I made a mistake." It’s "I am a failure and I hurt people." I mean, Mary and Susan were my friends, and I treated them like... like subordinates in some kind of corporate takeover. I just can't seem to forgive myself. I thought maybe after a few weeks, the sting would wear off, you know? Like it usually does when you have a disagreement or a project doesn't go perfectly. But it hasn't. It’s been nine months, and the guilt is just as fresh and just as heavy as it was the day Susan sent that email. I just feel so completely worthless, like I have nothing left to offer anyone, and I certainly didn't expect to feel *that* bad for *this* long.
Have you experienced any loss of interest in activities you normally enjoy during these past nine months?

Well, yes, absolutely. It's... it's like all the color has just drained out of everything I used to love doing. I mean, my garden, for instance. I used to be out there every single morning, practically at the crack of dawn, checking on the hydrangeas and making sure the soil pH was just right for the blue ones, because you know how tricky they can be if the soil gets too alkaline. I'd spend hours pulling weeds, pruning the rose bushes, just enjoying the quiet and the fresh air before the day really started. It was my sanctuary, really. But now? Now I look out the kitchen window at the flower beds, and they're completely overgrown, and I just... I don't care. I just feel nothing at all. 

And the quilting... oh, the quilting. That's the hardest part to talk about. I've been making my own quilt entries for the county fair for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. Every winter, I'd start planning my design, picking out the patterns, ordering these beautiful, specialized fabrics from catalogs... it was my passion. I'd get so excited when the seed catalogs and the fabric swatches would arrive in the mail in January. I'd sit at the dining room table with a cup of tea and just pore over them for hours, imagining all the possibilities. But lately, for these past nine months, those same catalogs have been piling up on the entryway table. I look at them, and I look at the stacks of fabric in my sewing room, and there's just... nothing. No spark, no interest, no desire to even touch them. It's like looking at a pile of rocks. It just feels so empty, you know? Like the part of me that used to get joy from creating things and growing things is just completely gone.
Have you had any days in the past nine months where you felt okay, or was the low mood constant?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I keep hoping I'll wake up one morning and the fog will have lifted, you know? Like I'll open my eyes and suddenly feel like making a cup of tea and walking out to check the hydrangeas like I used to. I keep waiting for that morning. But it just never comes. It's just this heavy, dark blanket every single day. 

I mean, if I really think about it, ever since everything started falling apart... since the fabric orders got so hopelessly behind schedule, and then all those awful conflicts with Mary and Susan just completely blew up in my face... I've just been stuck. It's been about nine months now, nine whole months of just sitting in this low, guilty place. There hasn't been a single day where I felt like myself again, not even for an hour. It's just constant. From the minute I wake up—usually way too early, mind you, and then I just lie there in the dark—to the minute I finally manage to fall asleep, it's just this endless loop of feeling worthless. Nine months is a long time to feel this way, doctor. It feels like a lifetime. I just keep waiting for a break in the clouds, but it's just been a solid wall of gray since the day that email went out.
Have you experienced any pleasure or enjoyment from activities, hobbies, or social interactions at all during these past nine months?

Like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor, it really is a complete blank. No pleasure at all, from anything or anyone. I know I just went on and on about the garden and the quilting, but it really is the starkest example I can give you of just how much joy I've lost. I mean, I used to absolutely love checking my garden every day, and working on my own quilt entries was my absolute pride and joy. It gave me such a sense of purpose. But lately, I just look at the fabric and those glossy seed catalogs that keep arriving in the mail, and I feel nothing much at all. 

And you asked about social interactions, too. Well, the thing is, the quilting and the gardening *were* social for me. I used to love chatting over the fence with my neighbor about his tomatoes versus my hydrangeas, or spending an hour at the fabric shop just talking with the other ladies about patterns and thread counts. It was a whole community. But now? If someone comes to the door, I just sit quietly in the living room and pretend I'm not home. I don't want to talk to anyone. 

My daughter actually came over a few weeks ago—bless her heart, she was trying so hard to cheer me up. She brought her tablet and tried to get me to look at this beautiful new line of autumn-themed fabrics she found online, because she knows how much I used to love planning my quilt entries for the fall. She sat right there at my kitchen table, scrolling through all these pictures, trying to get me to engage. And I just sat there staring at the screen. I knew I *should* think they were pretty, and I knew the old me would have already been calculating how many yards I needed for a border, but I just felt completely flat. Just like with the seed catalogs on the entryway table. I just looked at it all and felt... nothing. It's like my capacity for enjoyment has just been scooped right out of me, leaving this big, hollow space. So no, no pleasure at all. Not even a glimmer of it.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight since the project fell apart and you started feeling this way?

Well, weight changes... you know, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I suppose I haven't been paying much attention to the scale lately. It's funny you ask, though, because my daughter was just saying the other day that I looked a little different in my face, but I think that's just because I haven't been sleeping well and I have these dark circles under my eyes. But as for my actual weight, no, I don't think there's been any real change. 

I still make my meals out of habit, mostly. I'll get up and make a piece of toast with a little bit of butter—just a thin scrape, you know, because my husband used to always say I used too much butter, but I always liked the way it melted into the little nooks and crannies of English muffins, though I haven't bought English muffins in months. Anyway, I'll have my toast, and maybe a cup of tea, though half the time I forget about the tea and it goes cold on the counter while I'm just sitting there staring at the wall. And for dinner, I'll just heat up a can of soup. Chicken noodle, usually, or maybe tomato if I'm feeling adventurous, which I'm not. But I eat it. I just sit at the kitchen table, looking out at the overgrown garden, and I eat my soup. It doesn't taste like much of anything anymore, just sort of warm and salty, but I know I have to eat. 

So, no, my clothes still fit the same as they did nine months ago. I haven't had to take in any seams or buy new slacks or anything like that. My favorite navy blue trousers—the ones I used to wear when I'd go to the fabric store because they have those nice deep pockets for carrying my little notebook of measurements—they still button up just fine. So I'd have to say my weight has stayed pretty much exactly the same, despite everything else falling apart. It's just one of those things, I guess. You lose your joy, you lose your energy, but the scale stays exactly where it was.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself during these past nine months?

Well, harming myself... no. No, not in the way you mean. I don't have any sort of plan to actually do anything to hurt myself. I wouldn't do that. But... well, if I'm being completely honest with you, doctor, and I know I need to be... I do catch myself thinking about it in a different way. 

Like when I go to bed at night, after just sitting there all day feeling so useless, I pull the covers up and I just find myself hoping, really wishing, that maybe I just wouldn't wake up the next morning. It's not that I want to take a bunch of pills or do something violent, I don't have a plan like that at all. It's just... I catch myself thinking how much easier it would be for absolutely everyone if I just quietly slipped away in my sleep. 

Because right now, I'm just this terrible weight on everyone around me. You know, like my daughter coming over with her tablet, trying so hard to get a smile out of me, and I just give her nothing in return. It breaks my heart, but I can't fix it. And then there's the whole disaster with the quilt guild, all those unresolved, ugly feelings with Mary and Susan, and the fabric orders that I just completely ruined... it's a mess. It's just a giant, awful mess that I made, and I don't know how to clean it up. So I just lie there in the dark and think about how much simpler it would be if I just didn't wake up, and then nobody would have to deal with my mess anymore. They wouldn't have to worry about cheering me up or tiptoeing around my dark moods. They could all just move on. So, no plan to hurt myself, no, but... I do think about not being here. A lot, actually.
Do you ever have moments during the day where your low mood lifts, even if it's just for a little while?

Well, a moment where it lifts... I suppose you mean like a break in the clouds, where suddenly things feel a bit lighter? No. No, I don't really have moments like that anymore. It's just... it's a constant, heavy blanket over everything. I know some people might have a good hour here or there, maybe when the sun comes out or they have a nice cup of tea, but for me, it's just this continuous, flat grayness. 

I mean, I try, I really do. Like yesterday, my neighbor—the one with the tomatoes I mentioned earlier—he actually brought over a little basket of his first harvest. Beautiful, bright red cherry tomatoes. And he stood on the porch, and I made myself open the door and accept them, and I tried to muster up a smile and say thank you. I really tried to feel that little spark of neighborly connection that I used to enjoy so much. But even as I was holding this lovely little basket, and he was telling me about the new fertilizer he tried this year, I just felt... nothing. The whole time, I was just waiting for him to stop talking so I could close the door and go back to sitting in my chair. 

So, no, there isn't really any lifting of the mood. It's just the same low, heavy feeling from the moment I wake up—or from the moment I realize I've woken up and didn't just slip away like I hoped—until the moment I go back to sleep. It doesn't matter if it's a sunny afternoon or if someone brings me a gift, or if my daughter comes over. The feeling just sits there, right in my chest, and it doesn't budge. Not even for a minute. It's exhausting, honestly, just carrying it around all day with no relief. So, no, no moments of it lifting at all.
Do you ever feel like you're not in this low mood for even a brief moment during the day?

Well, I know I just said it doesn't lift, but I suppose you're asking if there's even a split second where it's not there... and I really have to say no, doctor. It's just... it's like a stain that won't wash out, no matter how hard you scrub. You know when you spill coffee on a white blouse? I had this beautiful white linen blouse, the one I wore to my niece's graduation, and I spilled coffee right down the front. I tried club soda, I tried bleach, I tried everything, and even when it faded, the shadow of it was still there, ruining the whole thing. That's what this feels like, but it's not a shadow, it's the whole stain, all the time. 

There isn't a single minute where I feel like myself again. Not even when I'm just doing mindless things, like folding laundry. I used to actually enjoy folding laundry, if you can believe it. Taking the warm towels out of the dryer, smoothing them out, making the edges meet perfectly... it was soothing. Now, I pull a towel out and it just feels heavy, and I fold it, and I'm just thinking about how pointless it all is, how I'm just going to use the towel and wash it and fold it again, over and over until I die. 

So, no, there isn't a brief moment. There's no reprieve. I don't suddenly look out the window and think, "Oh, what a lovely bird," and forget for a second how miserable I am. I look at the bird and think about how much energy it takes for it to fly, and how I don't even have the energy to stand up. It's just a constant, unbroken stretch of feeling completely hollowed out. From morning until night, every single day, without a single pause or break. It's just always there.
Are you able to perform your daily tasks and responsibilities despite feeling this low?

Perform my daily tasks... oh, doctor, no. Not at all. I mean, I wish I could say I was pushing through it, but I'm just... I'm not. My husband, bless his heart, he has had to take over absolutely everything around the house. The entire household routine has just fallen squarely on his shoulders. He's doing the grocery shopping, he's trying to figure out my filing system for the bills, he's even doing the laundry—which, like I mentioned before, I used to actually enjoy, but now I just sit in my chair while he's sorting the darks and the lights and trying to figure out which cycle to use for the delicates. It makes me feel terrible, watching him do all this after he's already been working, but I just can't seem to make myself get up and help him. 

And it's not just the house, either. It's everything outside the house, too. Like the historical society. I've been volunteering with them for years, and I had all these commitments. I was supposed to be organizing the spring archive display this year, coordinating the volunteers, getting the display cases ready at the library... but I just stopped. I completely stopped going, stopped answering their emails, stopped returning their calls. 

I just couldn't face them. I knew they were waiting on me, I knew they needed the keys to the display cabinets and the catalog notes I had been working on, but the thought of actually walking in there and looking at their faces... having to explain why I hadn't done a single thing I promised to do... it was just too much. I couldn't bear the thought of them looking at me and seeing this completely useless person. So my husband had to step in and deal with them, too. He actually had to drive down to the historical society building, hand over my binders and the keys, and make up some excuse for me. It's humiliating, really, having your husband go clean up your messes and apologize to people because you can't even put on a pair of shoes and face the people who are relying on you. So he's doing the cooking, the cleaning, the apologizing... all of it. Because I just can't do any of it.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with family or friends since you started feeling this way?

Changes in my relationships... well, I suppose the biggest change is just that I'm not really having them anymore. I mean, I'm just not seeing anyone. It's not that I've had some big falling out or that people are angry with me, although I wouldn't blame them if they were, especially the ladies at the historical society. It's just that I've completely withdrawn. 

Take my friend Susan, for example. We've been friends since our girls were in kindergarten together, and we used to meet for coffee every single Tuesday morning at that little bakery downtown, the one with the good almond croissants. We've done that for years. But since this... this heavy feeling started, I just can't bring myself to go. At first, I'd make excuses—saying I had a headache, or that we were expecting a delivery, or that my husband needed the car, even though he takes the train. I hated lying to her, but the thought of sitting across from her, trying to sip coffee and pretend to care about her daughter's new kitchen renovation or whatever neighborhood gossip she had... it just felt impossible. 

And then eventually, I just stopped answering her calls altogether. I'd see her name pop up on my phone, and my stomach would just tie itself into knots, and I'd watch it ring until it went to voicemail. I must have a dozen voicemails from her just sitting there, asking if I'm alright, asking if I want her to come over. But I don't want her to come over. I don't want anyone to see me like this, sitting in my chair all day in yesterday's clothes. 

And it's the same with my daughter, Emily. She usually comes over for Sunday dinner. I used to love cooking for her, making a nice roast or her favorite lasagna. But now, my husband has had to tell her not to come, or he'll go meet her for lunch somewhere without me. When she does call, I let him answer it. I can hear him in the hallway, speaking in that hushed, careful voice he uses now, telling her that Mom is just having a rough day and needs to rest. It breaks my heart to know I'm pushing them all away, but I just don't have the energy to maintain the connections. I feel like a ghost in my own life, just sort of haunting the house while everyone else goes on living. So, yes, things have changed completely, mostly because I've just vanished from everyone's lives.
Do you ever have even a brief moment where you feel like your normal self again?

Well, like I was saying just a moment ago, doctor, I really don't. I know it's probably hard to believe that there isn't even a tiny window, but there just isn't. My normal self... well, my normal self was the kind of woman who would be up at the crack of dawn. I'd have the coffee brewing, I'd be out on the porch watering the ferns before the heat of the day set in, just listening to the neighborhood wake up. I always loved mornings. 

You'd think that maybe, just maybe, in those first few seconds of waking up, before my brain fully turns on and remembers everything, I might feel like that woman again. Just for a heartbeat. But I don't. The second my eyes open, before I even fully realize I'm awake, that terrible, crushing weight is already there. It's like... you know when you go to the dentist, and they put that heavy lead apron over your chest to take the X-rays? How it just presses you down into the vinyl chair and makes it a little hard to take a deep breath? That's exactly how I wake up feeling, and nobody comes to take the apron off. 

It doesn't lift for a single second all day. I sit in my chair and I keep waiting for just a crack in the clouds, just one minute where I can breathe freely and feel like the old me, but it's just solid gray. There's no fluctuation. It doesn't matter if it's a beautiful sunny afternoon or if my favorite movie is playing on the television—which I can't even pay attention to anyway. The feeling is completely static. So, no, to answer your question again, there really aren't any moments at all where I feel like myself. I honestly can't even remember what feeling like myself actually feels like anymore, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. It feels like that person is just completely gone.
Do you feel like your low mood has stayed exactly the same since it started, without any variation at all?

Yes, exactly. Like I was just trying to say, it really hasn't shifted an inch. Not one inch. I know it's hard to wrap your mind around—even my husband struggles to understand it. He keeps trying to find these little victories, you know? He'll say, "Oh, you ate half your toast this morning, you must be feeling a bit lighter," or "You sat in the living room while Jeopardy was on, that's an improvement!" 

But he doesn't understand that I'm just chewing the toast because he put it right in my hand, and my eyes are just pointed in the general direction of the television. I'm not actually watching it. Inside, the level of... of just absolute emptiness and heaviness, it's exactly the same. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday or a Saturday, morning or midnight. It's been this exact same depth, this exact same weight, ever since it settled over me. 

You'd expect a mood to be like a wave, wouldn't you? You'd expect it to crest and fall, maybe be a little worse on a rainy day and a little better when you get a nice phone call. But it's not a wave. It's just... still water. Dark, heavy, completely still water. It doesn't ripple. So, no, to be perfectly clear, there hasn't been any variation at all. It's just one long, continuous stretch of exactly the same feeling.
Do you think your current low mood is related to the guilt and shame you feel about the historical society project, or is it something that you feel is separate from that?

Oh, it's absolutely related, doctor. I don't think I can even separate the two things in my mind anymore. It's just this constant, miserable loop in my head. I sit in that chair I told you about, the one in the living room, and while my husband thinks I'm resting or watching television, all I'm actually doing is playing back everything that happened with that project. Over and over and over again. 

I just sit there, day after day, and I keep going over every late order... you know, the commemorative materials we were supposed to have ready for the summer festival. They were weeks late, and I was the one in charge of the vendor coordination, so it fell squarely on my shoulders. And then, because I was so panicked and overwhelmed about the shipments being delayed, I was just awful to the people who were only trying to help me. I keep replaying every sharp thing I said to the volunteers. Mary and Helen were just trying to help unpack the boxes when they finally did arrive, and I snapped at them like they were disobedient children. I can still see the shocked look on Helen's face, and it just eats away at me.

I had my big notebook out, making these massive, detailed schedules for everyone, assigning shifts and tasks. And you have to understand, quilting takes a tremendous amount of time, it's not something you just whip up in an afternoon, but I was just so absolutely sure I could do it all. A lot, actually.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is consistently present throughout the day
doctor.question: Do you ever have moments during the day where your low mood lifts, even if it's just for a little while?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about mood reactivity (whether the low mood lifts temporarily), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, a moment where it lifts... I suppose you mean like a break in the clouds, where suddenly things feel a bit lighter? No. No, I don't really have moments like that anymore. It's just... it's a constant, heavy blanket over everything. I know some people might have a good hour here or there, maybe when the sun comes out or they have a nice cup of tea, but for me, it's just this continuous, flat grayness. 

I mean, I try, I really do. Like yesterday, my neighbor—the one with the tomatoes I mentioned earlier—he actually brought over a little basket of his first harvest. Beautiful, bright red cherry tomatoes. And he stood on the porch, and I made myself open the door and accept them, and I tried to muster up a smile and say thank you. I really tried to feel that little spark of neighborly connection that I used to enjoy so much. But even as I was holding this lovely little basket, and he was telling me about the new fertilizer he tried this year, I just felt... nothing. The whole time, I was just waiting for him to stop talking so I could close the door and go back to sitting in my chair. 

So, no, there isn't really any lifting of the mood. It's just the same low, heavy feeling from the moment I wake up—or from the moment I realize I've woken up and didn't just slip away like I hoped—until the moment I go back to sleep. It doesn't matter if it's a sunny afternoon or if someone brings me a gift, or if my daughter comes over. The feeling just sits there, right in my chest, and it doesn't budge. Not even for a minute. It's exhausting, honestly, just carrying it around all day with no relief. So, no, no moments of it lifting at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is consistently present throughout the day
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're not in this low mood for even a brief moment during the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about mood reactivity or whether the depressed mood ever lifts, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I know I just said it doesn't lift, but I suppose you're asking if there's even a split second where it's not there... and I really have to say no, doctor. It's just... it's like a stain that won't wash out, no matter how hard you scrub. You know when you spill coffee on a white blouse? I had this beautiful white linen blouse, the one I wore to my niece's graduation, and I spilled coffee right down the front. I tried club soda, I tried bleach, I tried everything, and even when it faded, the shadow of it was still there, ruining the whole thing. That's what this feels like, but it's not a shadow, it's the whole stain, all the time. 

There isn't a single minute where I feel like myself again. Not even when I'm just doing mindless things, like folding laundry. I used to actually enjoy folding laundry, if you can believe it. Taking the warm towels out of the dryer, smoothing them out, making the edges meet perfectly... it was soothing. Now, I pull a towel out and it just feels heavy, and I fold it, and I'm just thinking about how pointless it all is, how I'm just going to use the towel and wash it and fold it again, over and over until I die. 

So, no, there isn't a brief moment. There's no reprieve. I don't suddenly look out the window and think, "Oh, what a lovely bird," and forget for a second how miserable I am. I look at the bird and think about how much energy it takes for it to fly, and how I don't even have the energy to stand up. It's just a constant, unbroken stretch of feeling completely hollowed out. From morning until night, every single day, without a single pause or break. It's just always there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is significantly impacting their daily functioning
doctor.question: Are you able to perform your daily tasks and responsibilities despite feeling this low?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My husband has had to take over household routines and deal with the historical society because I stopped keeping commitments and couldn’t face the people waiting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to perform daily tasks and responsibilities, which directly relates to my functional impairment where my husband has had to take over household routines.

patient.answer:
Perform my daily tasks... oh, doctor, no. Not at all. I mean, I wish I could say I was pushing through it, but I'm just... I'm not. My husband, bless his heart, he has had to take over absolutely everything around the house. The entire household routine has just fallen squarely on his shoulders. He's doing the grocery shopping, he's trying to figure out my filing system for the bills, he's even doing the laundry—which, like I mentioned before, I used to actually enjoy, but now I just sit in my chair while he's sorting the darks and the lights and trying to figure out which cycle to use for the delicates. It makes me feel terrible, watching him do all this after he's already been working, but I just can't seem to make myself get up and help him. 

And it's not just the house, either. It's everything outside the house, too. Like the historical society. I've been volunteering with them for years, and I had all these commitments. I was supposed to be organizing the spring archive display this year, coordinating the volunteers, getting the display cases ready at the library... but I just stopped. I completely stopped going, stopped answering their emails, stopped returning their calls. 

I just couldn't face them. I knew they were waiting on me, I knew they needed the keys to the display cabinets and the catalog notes I had been working on, but the thought of actually walking in there and looking at their faces... having to explain why I hadn't done a single thing I promised to do... it was just too much. I couldn't bear the thought of them looking at me and seeing this completely useless person. So my husband had to step in and deal with them, too. He actually had to drive down to the historical society building, hand over my binders and the keys, and make up some excuse for me. It's humiliating, really, having your husband go clean up your messes and apologize to people because you can't even put on a pair of shoes and face the people who are relying on you. So he's doing the cooking, the cleaning, the apologizing... all of it. Because I just can't do any of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is significantly interfering with their social relationships
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with family or friends since you started feeling this way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in relationships with family or friends. While my profile mentions my husband taking over duties and me avoiding volunteers (Functional Impairment) or feeling guilty about snapping at volunteers (Worthlessness/Guilt), there is no distinct symptom in my profile specifically dedicated to relationship changes.

patient.answer:
Changes in my relationships... well, I suppose the biggest change is just that I'm not really having them anymore. I mean, I'm just not seeing anyone. It's not that I've had some big falling out or that people are angry with me, although I wouldn't blame them if they were, especially the ladies at the historical society. It's just that I've completely withdrawn. 

Take my friend Susan, for example. We've been friends since our girls were in kindergarten together, and we used to meet for coffee every single Tuesday morning at that little bakery downtown, the one with the good almond croissants. We've done that for years. But since this... this heavy feeling started, I just can't bring myself to go. At first, I'd make excuses—saying I had a headache, or that we were expecting a delivery, or that my husband needed the car, even though he takes the train. I hated lying to her, but the thought of sitting across from her, trying to sip coffee and pretend to care about her daughter's new kitchen renovation or whatever neighborhood gossip she had... it just felt impossible. 

And then eventually, I just stopped answering her calls altogether. I'd see her name pop up on my phone, and my stomach would just tie itself into knots, and I'd watch it ring until it went to voicemail. I must have a dozen voicemails from her just sitting there, asking if I'm alright, asking if I want her to come over. But I don't want her to come over. I don't want anyone to see me like this, sitting in my chair all day in yesterday's clothes. 

And it's the same with my daughter, Emily. She usually comes over for Sunday dinner. I used to love cooking for her, making a nice roast or her favorite lasagna. But now, my husband has had to tell her not to come, or he'll go meet her for lunch somewhere without me. When she does call, I let him answer it. I can hear him in the hallway, speaking in that hushed, careful voice he uses now, telling her that Mom is just having a rough day and needs to rest. It breaks my heart to know I'm pushing them all away, but I just don't have the energy to maintain the connections. I feel like a ghost in my own life, just sort of haunting the house while everyone else goes on living. So, yes, things have changed completely, mostly because I've just vanished from everyone's lives.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is persistent and unrelenting
doctor.question: Do you ever have even a brief moment where you feel like your normal self again?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about mood reactivity (whether the low mood ever lifts briefly), which is not covered by any specific item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying just a moment ago, doctor, I really don't. I know it's probably hard to believe that there isn't even a tiny window, but there just isn't. My normal self... well, my normal self was the kind of woman who would be up at the crack of dawn. I'd have the coffee brewing, I'd be out on the porch watering the ferns before the heat of the day set in, just listening to the neighborhood wake up. I always loved mornings. 

You'd think that maybe, just maybe, in those first few seconds of waking up, before my brain fully turns on and remembers everything, I might feel like that woman again. Just for a heartbeat. But I don't. The second my eyes open, before I even fully realize I'm awake, that terrible, crushing weight is already there. It's like... you know when you go to the dentist, and they put that heavy lead apron over your chest to take the X-rays? How it just presses you down into the vinyl chair and makes it a little hard to take a deep breath? That's exactly how I wake up feeling, and nobody comes to take the apron off. 

It doesn't lift for a single second all day. I sit in my chair and I keep waiting for just a crack in the clouds, just one minute where I can breathe freely and feel like the old me, but it's just solid gray. There's no fluctuation. It doesn't matter if it's a beautiful sunny afternoon or if my favorite movie is playing on the television—which I can't even pay attention to anyway. The feeling is completely static. So, no, to answer your question again, there really aren't any moments at all where I feel like myself. I honestly can't even remember what feeling like myself actually feels like anymore, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. It feels like that person is just completely gone.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is persistent and unchanging
doctor.question: Do you feel like your low mood has stayed exactly the same since it started, without any variation at all?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about mood variation or mood reactivity (whether the low mood fluctuates), which is not covered by any of the specific symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer:
Yes, exactly. Like I was just trying to say, it really hasn't shifted an inch. Not one inch. I know it's hard to wrap your mind around—even my husband struggles to understand it. He keeps trying to find these little victories, you know? He'll say, "Oh, you ate half your toast this morning, you must be feeling a bit lighter," or "You sat in the living room while Jeopardy was on, that's an improvement!" 

But he doesn't understand that I'm just chewing the toast because he put it right in my hand, and my eyes are just pointed in the general direction of the television. I'm not actually watching it. Inside, the level of... of just absolute emptiness and heaviness, it's exactly the same. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday or a Saturday, morning or midnight. It's been this exact same depth, this exact same weight, ever since it settled over me. 

You'd expect a mood to be like a wave, wouldn't you? You'd expect it to crest and fall, maybe be a little worse on a rainy day and a little better when you get a nice phone call. But it's not a wave. It's just... still water. Dark, heavy, completely still water. It doesn't ripple. So, no, to be perfectly clear, there hasn't been any variation at all. It's just one long, continuous stretch of exactly the same feeling.

patient.answer:
Oh, it's absolutely related, doctor. I don't think I can even separate the two things in my mind anymore. It's just this constant, miserable loop in my head. I sit in that chair I told you about, the one in the living room, and while my husband thinks I'm resting or watching television, all I'm actually doing is playing back everything that happened with that project. Over and over and over again. 

I just sit there, day after day, and I keep going over every late order... you know, the commemorative materials we were supposed to have ready for the summer festival. They were weeks late, and I was the one in charge of the vendor coordination, so it fell squarely on my shoulders. And then, because I was so panicked and overwhelmed about the shipments being delayed, I was just awful to the people who were only trying to help me. I keep replaying every sharp thing I said to the volunteers. Mary and Helen were just trying to help unpack the boxes when they finally did arrive, and I snapped at them like they were disobedient children. I can still see the shocked look on Helen's face, and it just eats away at me. 

It's this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest, telling myself I let the church down—because they were kind enough to let us use the fellowship hall for all the sorting and organizing—and I let the historical society down after they trusted me with the biggest fundraiser we've had in a decade. Honestly, I feel like I let this whole town down. I know that might sound dramatic to someone on the outside, but in a community this size, people remember things like that. They remember who ruined the festival preparations and who drove away the best volunteers. 

And the guilt of it, the absolute shame of knowing how incompetent I was, how mean I was to my friends... it just presses down on me right along with that heavy lead apron feeling I mentioned before. I can't forgive myself for it. I just keep thinking, what kind of person behaves like that? What kind of woman ruins a community event and alienates her peers over some delayed shipping boxes? So, yes, the low mood and the guilt, they are just completely tied together in this awful, tight knot that I can't seem to undo. If I had just called the supplier a week earlier, maybe none of this would have happened, and I wouldn't be sitting here feeling like such a complete and utter failure...
